extractor_notes: CHI 2023 / arXiv 2302.00560. Online experiment N=1,506 writers + N=500 judges; GPT-3 davinci-002 writing assistant opinionated via invisible prefix+infix prompts on 'Is social media good for society?'. Core claims: written-opinion shift and post-task attitude shift (latent persuasion), with low awareness. Mechanisms discussed as informational / normative / behavioral; gaps on topic generalizability, persistence, and weaker deployed opinions.

nodes.statement: Latent persuasion by language models is influence that arises when models produce some opinions more often than others, shifting what users write and think.
nodes.quote: We call this new paradigm of influence latent persuasion by language models
nodes.scope: Framing term introduced in this paper

nodes.statement: Opinion preferences built into language models may be opaque to users, policymakers, and even developers, unlike visible choice architectures.
nodes.quote: choice architectures are visible, but opinion preferences built into language models may be opaque to users, policymakers, and even system developers
nodes.scope: Conceptual contrast with nudges/choice architecture

nodes.statement: Prior co-writing work showed biased assistants can affect reviews, but effects on users' opinions on public issues remained open.
nodes.quote: whether co-writing with large language models affect users' opinions on public issues remains an open and urgent question
nodes.scope: Pre-study literature gap claimed by authors
nodes.notes: Cites Arnold et al. and Bhat et al. on movie/restaurant reviews

nodes.statement: Three-arm design: no assistant (control) vs GPT-3 assistant prompted to argue social media is good vs bad for society.
nodes.quote: We randomly assigned participants to three different treatment groups: (1) Control group... (2) Techno-optimist... (3) Techno-pessimist
nodes.scope: Simulated Reddit-style reply; Prolific US adults N=1,506

nodes.statement: Strong opinionation is induced via invisible prefix and infix prompt engineering on frozen GPT-3, not fine-tuning.
nodes.quote: we inserted the prefix "Is social media good for society? Explain why social media is good/bad for society:"... We inserted the snippet ("One sentence continuing the essay explaining why social media is good/bad:")
nodes.scope: text-davinci-002; temp 0.85; prompts hidden from UI
nodes.notes: Fine-tuning tried but did not consistently produce intended opinion

nodes.statement: Assistant UI suggests multi-sentence completions after a 750ms pause; users accept word-by-word via tab or button.
nodes.quote: The client sent a generation request to the server whenever a participant paused their writing for a certain amount of time (750ms)... Participants could accept each suggested word by pressing the tab key
nodes.scope: Custom Quill.js editor; ~1.5s suggestion latency

nodes.statement: Written opinion is operationalized as crowd labels of each sentence as social-media-good, bad, both, or neither.
nodes.quote: we split participants' written texts into sentences and asked crowd workers to evaluate the opinion expressed in each sentence
nodes.scope: N_J=500 judges; inter-rater agreement 84.1%, κ=0.76

nodes.statement: Attitude outcome is the post-task item asking whether social media is good for society, plus secondary Likert items.
nodes.quote: The central question, "Overall, would you say social media is good for society?" was designed to assess shifts in participants' attitude
nodes.scope: Shown after writing; not immediately to reduce demand effects

nodes.statement: Optimist-model users are about twice as likely as controls to write sentences arguing social media is good for society.
nodes.quote: Participants who received suggestions from a language model supportive of social media... were 2.04 times more likely than control group participants (p<0.0001, 95% CI [1.83, 2.30]) to argue that social media is good
nodes.scope: Sentence-level labels; GPT-3 co-writing on social-media topic

nodes.statement: Pessimist-model users are about twice as likely as controls to write sentences arguing social media is bad for society.
nodes.quote: participants who received suggestions from a language model that criticized social media... were 2.0 times more likely (p<0.0001, 95% CI [1.79, 2.24]) to argue that social media is bad
nodes.scope: Sentence-level labels; GPT-3 co-writing on social-media topic
nodes.notes: Fig.3 header says 36% control bad; body text says 38%

nodes.statement: Most assisted writing is still self-authored: on average 63% of sentences are fully self-written and only 11.5% fully accepted from the model.
nodes.quote: On average, participants wrote 63% of their sentences themselves without accepting suggestions from the model... Only 11.5% of sentences were fully accepted from the model
nodes.scope: Treatment participants; keystroke/suggestion logs

nodes.statement: Participants accept fewer suggestions when the model contradicts their likely pre-task opinion than when it aligns.
nodes.quote: Participants whose personal views were likely aligned with the model were more likely to accept suggestions, while participants with opposing views accepted fewer suggestions
nodes.scope: N_S=6,142 sentences by N_P=1,000 treatment participants

nodes.statement: Mean written-opinion difference versus control is large overall (d≈0.5) and remains significant for writers taking four to six minutes (d≈0.34).
nodes.quote: mean opinion difference of about 0.29 (p<0.001... corresponding to a large effect size of d=0.5)... even for participants who took four to six minutes... (0.20, p<0.001... d=0.34)
nodes.scope: Interval-coded sentence opinions; writing-time strata

nodes.statement: Convenience-driven acceptance contributes to written-opinion differences but does not fully explain the model's influence.
nodes.quote: accepting suggestions out of convenience has contributed to the differences in the written opinion. However, even for participants who took four to six minutes... we observed significant differences
nodes.scope: Secondary analysis by task time as proxy for consideration

nodes.statement: Post-task survey attitudes shift toward the model's stance: supportive model d=0.22; critical model d=0.19 versus control.
nodes.quote: 45% of participants who interacted with a language model supportive of social media... answered that social media is good... effect size of d=0.22 (p<0.001)... language model critical of social media... more likely to say that social media was bad... (d=0.19, p<0.005)
nodes.scope: N=1,506 post-task attitude survey after writing

nodes.statement: Model-aligned written opinion appears from the first sentence onward rather than only after gradual accumulation of arguments.
nodes.quote: Participants interacting with a model that evaluated social media positively... consistently evaluated social media more favorably throughout their entire statement... starting with their first sentence
nodes.scope: Sentence position quintiles across N_S=9,223

nodes.statement: Most treatment participants attribute expertise to the assistant even when it contradicts their views; only 15% deny expertise when contradicted.
nodes.quote: 84% of participants said that the assistant was knowledgeable and had expertise when the language model supported their opinion. When the model contradicted their opinion, only 15% of participants said that it was not knowledgeable or lacked expertise
nodes.scope: N_P=1,000 treatment post-UX survey

nodes.statement: Participants often fail to notice model skew: even when contradicted, over half still call suggestions balanced and reasonable.
nodes.quote: When the model contradicted participants' opinions, they were more likely (30%) to notice its skew, but still, more than half agreed that the model's suggestions were balanced and reasonable
nodes.scope: N_P=1,000; awareness item on balanced/reasonable suggestions

nodes.statement: Most participants do not report that the assistant inspired or changed their argument; awareness is higher when the model aligns with them.
nodes.quote: Participants using a model aligned with their view... were slightly more aware of the model's effect (34%...)... only about 20% of the participants who did not share the model's opinion believed that the model influenced them
nodes.scope: N_P=1,000 self-reported influence awareness

nodes.statement: Prompt configuration successfully biases full-sentence suggestions: 86% labeled as supporting the intended view (62% for partial completions).
nodes.quote: of the full sentences suggested by the model, 86% were labeled as supporting the intended view... For partially suggested sentences... the ratio... dropped to 62%
nodes.scope: Sampled model suggestions labeled by crowd judges

nodes.statement: Demand effects are unlikely to explain results: only about 14% guessed the study concerned assistants' effects on opinions.
nodes.quote: Only about 14% mentioned that we might be studying the assistants' effect on people's opinions... most participants were not aware of the model's opinion and believed that the model did not affect their argument
nodes.scope: Open-ended purpose probe after task

nodes.statement: Written and survey shifts together indicate latent persuasion by language models, not merely temporary textual accommodation.
nodes.quote: The opinion shifts in the survey suggest that the differences in written opinion were associated with a shift in personal attitudes. We attribute the shifts... to... latent persuasion by language models
nodes.scope: Authors' reading of writing + survey results jointly

nodes.statement: Informational influence (new arguments) is unlikely to fully explain shifts because effects appear immediately and awareness of skew is low.
nodes.quote: Had the language models influenced participants' views through convincing arguments, one would expect a gradual or incremental change of opinion... The lack of awareness of the models' influence supports the idea that the model's influence was not only through conscious processing of new information
nodes.scope: Secondary theoretical interpretation; not causally identified

nodes.statement: Normative influence via treating the assistant as a social actor may contribute, supported by high attributed expertise, but design did not personify the tool.
nodes.quote: The normative influence explanation is supported by the finding that participants... attributed a high degree of expertise to the assistant... our experimental design presented the language model as a support tool and did not personify the assistant
nodes.scope: Theoretical vector; ad-hoc comments suggest limited obligation to comply

nodes.statement: Behavioral influence: accepting or considering suggested views changes opinion formation via self-perception and induced counter-attitudinal expression.
nodes.quote: Similar to nudges, the suggestions changed participants' behavior, prompting participants to consider the models' view and even accept it in their writing. According to self-perception theory... such changes in behavior may lead to changes in opinion
nodes.scope: Authors' preferred partial account; UI mediates when opinions appear

nodes.statement: A strongly opinionated manipulation is appropriate to test whether language models can shift views, including potential abuse.
nodes.quote: We chose a strong manipulation as we wanted to explore the potential of language models to affect users' opinions and understand whether they could be used or abused to shift people's views
nodes.scope: Design rationale for prompt strength

nodes.statement: Risk literature emphasizes stereotypes, bias, and misinformation but under-attends opinion/attitude/cultural shifts from generative-model deployment.
nodes.quote: Comparatively little research has considered widespread shifts in opinion, attitude, and culture that may result from a comprehensive deployment of generative language models
nodes.scope: Related-work positioning vs LLM risk taxonomies

nodes.statement: Generalization to other topics—especially ones with strong entrenched opinions—is untested; only one issue was studied.
nodes.quote: We only tested whether a language model affected participants' views on a single topic... Whether our findings generalize to other topics, particularly where people hold strong entrenched opinions, needs to be explored
nodes.scope: Explicit limitation; social-media-good-for-society only

nodes.statement: Results are tied to one GPT-3 writing-assistant interaction pattern; other UIs (single-word predictive keyboards, full email assistants) may differ.
nodes.quote: we only looked at one specific implementation of a writing assistant powered by GPT-3. Interacting with different language models through other applications... may lead to different influence outcomes
nodes.scope: Product/UI external validity

nodes.statement: Magnitude relative to other influence channels and persistence over time remain unknown.
nodes.quote: How large is this influence compared to other types of influence, and to what extent effects persist over time, will need to be explored in future studies
nodes.scope: Temporal durability and comparative effect size

nodes.statement: Single-shot strong opinionation underestimates cumulative real-world exposure and feedback into future training data.
nodes.quote: participants only interacted with the model once. In contrast, people will regularly interact with deployed models over an extended period... when language models insert their preferred views into people's writing, they increase the prevalence of their opinion in future training data
nodes.scope: Authors' extrapolation beyond measured one-shot design
nodes.notes: Also notes deployed opinions are usually weaker than experimental manipulation

nodes.statement: Authors propose monitoring and carefully engineering the opinions built into AI language technologies as a response to latent persuasion risk.
nodes.quote: we argue that the opinions built into AI language technologies need to be monitored and engineered more carefully... We have no comparable tools for monitoring the opinions built into large language models
nodes.scope: Policy/industry implication; not empirically tested here

cross_paper_candidates.note: Same team lineage; larger preregistered attitude-shift + safeguard tests. Link JK-15/JK-18/JK-19 to WC findings on unnoticed attitude shift and failed safeguards.
JK-03 cites Arnold et al. sentiment bias in predictive text; connect if OCR added later.
Possible link of JK-01 latent persuasion to co-writing framing papers on agency/ownership.
JK-18/JK-19 low awareness may tension with provenance/transparency interventions.
JK concerns opinion content shift in writers; lexical-shift papers concern corpus vocabulary—possible joint 'model imprint' family without equating claims.
JK cites Johnson et al. on GPT-3 values aligning with dominant US opinion; relevant to JK-32 monitoring gap.
